content.text:
When your child pushes the veggies away

At the dinner table, do the green broccoli and orange carrots always end up nudged to the edge of the plate? Many parents have sighed while watching their child pick out only the white rice and the meat.

In fact, when a 4-to-5-year-old refuses unfamiliar vegetables, it isn't naughtiness — it's a natural part of development. So rather than scolding, a single story that makes your child want to reach for vegetables on their own is far more powerful.

Curious about the story of this toddler picky-eating book? We look at the lessons of this toddler picky-eating storybook alongside the pictures. Meet the key scenes of the story, too. Read this toddler picky-eating storybook with your child and talk it over together. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "Eat Every Color and Feel the Rainbow Power!" — how to fix picky eating in kids, the child who won't eat vegetables, building the habit of eating a variety of foods, and more.
content.caption: Refusing vegetables isn't naughtiness — it's a natural part of development.

content.alt: 01. Eat Every Color and Feel the Rainbow Power! - Why eating a variety of foods matters
content.text:
Why eating a variety of foods matters

Eating a variety of foods isn't just table manners — it's the foundation of a child's growth. Vegetables and fruits of different colors each carry different nutrients, so the more variety a child eats, the stronger and more energetic their body becomes.

What a child needs at this stage isn't a nutrition lecture, but the experience that vegetables aren't scary. The courage of one taste leads to the next challenge, and those small successes add up to slowly ease the picky eating.
content.caption: Vegetables of different colors each carry different nutrients.

content.alt: 01. Eat Every Color and Feel the Rainbow Power! - Hori's rainbow garden story
content.text:
Hori's rainbow garden story

The hero of "Eat Every Color and Feel the Rainbow Power!" is Hori, a baby tiger who loves only white rice and meat. The day after pushing his vegetables away, Hori strangely has no energy at all.

Just then, his friend Kongi the squirrel takes Hori to the rainbow vegetable garden. Red for strong, orange for sparkle, green for growing tall! Listening to the hidden color-power story of each vegetable, Hori gulps with anticipation and finally takes a crunchy bite of an orange carrot. Huh? It's sweeter than he thought!
content.caption: The hidden color-power story of each vegetable gives Hori courage.

content.alt: 01. Eat Every Color and Feel the Rainbow Power! - Putting varied eating into practice at home
content.text:
Putting varied eating into practice at home

Once you've read the story, it's time to put it into practice at the table. Here are a few ideas.

First, make a "rainbow plate of the day." Placing red, orange, green, and yellow each in its own section and treating it like a color game makes vegetables feel less scary. Second, praise a "one-bite challenge" in a big way. Even if they don't finish, the key is to recognize the courage of a single taste. Third, point to the vegetables and say their color names together. Their vocabulary grows naturally.
content.caption: Turn vegetables into a color game with a rainbow plate of the day.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. What should I do when my child is a picky eater?

A. Rather than forcing them to eat, share the imaginative idea that eating a variety of colorful vegetables gives you power, likening them to the colors of a rainbow. Praising even a single new bite in a big way is the first step to reducing picky eating.

Q. Do toddler picky-eating storybooks really help?

A. Watching the hero of the story happily eat new foods, a child naturally wants to do the same. A toddler picky-eating storybook helps reduce mealtime struggles and shows the joy of eating.

Q. How should I offer vegetables my child dislikes?

A. Rather than serving a large amount from the start, offer just a tiny bit, alongside a dish they like. Talking about colors and shapes like a game and letting them taste without pressure helps them get used to it little by little.
